title.said: Throw, and catch. Exceptions, in C plus plus.

a0.said: A tank, a level sensor, and a pump. Every cycle, the program reads the level and decides whether the pump should run.

a1.said: Inside, the program is a stack of calls: main runs a cycle, the cycle reads the level, and that means parsing the sensor's text.

a2.said: Most days the sensor sends a number. It is handed back down, floor by floor. The tank is full enough, so the pump stays off.

a3.said: But one day the sensor sends text. There is no number to hand back.

b1.said: The old answer is a special value. Minus one, say. And every floor on the way down has to check for it.

b2.said: One floor forgets, and the error walks through, dressed as a number. The pump starts, and the tank overflows.

c1.said: C plus plus has another way. The function that finds the problem throws.

c2.said: Nothing is returned. The call is abandoned, and its floor is gone.

c3.said: The exception falls, and every floor it passes goes the same way, unless that floor catches it. This is unwinding.

c4.said: As each floor goes, its local objects are destroyed. The destructors run, just as on a normal return.

d1.said: In main, a try block is waiting, with a catch for this type of exception.

d2.said: The error lands there, with its message intact. The pump stays off, and the program goes on.

e1.said: And if nobody catches it? The exception falls through main as well, and the program is terminated on the spot.

e2.said: Nothing was closed: the destructors never ran. So catch the exception where something can be done about it.

z1.said: Throw where the problem is found. Catch where it can be handled. The floors in between fall away, and clean up as they go.
